script.opening: (Earnest, a bit anxious, speaking from her desk.) "I'm just exhausted all the time, doctor — it's been months. I drag myself through work and crash at the weekend. I keep thinking something must be really wrong with me. Can you just test me for everything — my thyroid, my iron, anything — and find out what it is?"

facts.text: About four months. "No energy, mostly. Heavy. And I don't sleep well." Not falling asleep in the day. No muscle weakness. Feels worse after a bad night, not specifically after exercise.
"I'm on my laptop until late, then I lie there with my mind racing. I wake up feeling like I haven't slept." Bed about 1 am, up at 7. No snoring she knows of.
If asked: "No, none of those" — no weight loss, night sweats, fevers, lumps, bleeding or bruising, breathlessness, palpitations, change in bowels, thirst or passing more urine.
Regular, not heavy. Not pregnant — "I don't think so. I'm happy to do a test if it helps rule it out." Has a progestogen implant.
"I don't think so. I just feel flat most of the time." If asked about enjoyment: "I suppose I've been a bit flat. I haven't really thought of it like that." Worries a lot. No thoughts of self-harm.
"Lots of coffee to get through the day" — 5–6 cups plus an energy drink. "Not much alcohol" — a few glasses at weekends. Non-smoker. Stopped going to the gym. Diet: lots of snacks at her desk.
Software developer. "Work's been full-on. Deadlines, long hours, always on my phone. I haven't had a proper break in ages." Moved to a new city a year ago; few friends nearby. Single.
No regular medicines apart from the implant. No allergies. No family history of thyroid or coeliac disease she knows of.

Keen on tests: "As long as we do the tests." If asked what she fears: "Honestly? Something serious. You read things online and it's always something awful. I just want someone to find it." If told "it's just stress", feel dismissed and push back: "So you think I'm making it up?" If the doctor explains a focused set of tests and also explores life, accept: "Okay, that makes sense." Ask once: "Why not everything, though? Just to be sure?"

ice.ideas: "Something must be really wrong — the tests will find it."
ice.concerns: HIDDEN AGENDA — she fears a serious illness she has read about online; underneath, months of work stress, poor sleep and loneliness since moving that she hasn't connected to the tiredness.

cues: "I keep thinking something must be really wrong." — invites "what are you worried it might be?"
"I haven't had a proper break in ages." — the work and life story.

checkpoints.text: Takes fatigue seriously with a STRUCTURED history — nature (sleepiness vs energy vs muscle), duration, pattern, functional impact — and screens RED FLAGS (weight loss, fevers/night sweats, lymphadenopathy, breathlessness, neurological/focal symptoms, bleeding, progressive course)

Orders a FOCUSED, evidence-based first-line screen (FBC — very urgently, within 48 hours, per NICE NG12 for persistent fatigue — ferritin, TFTs, HbA1c/glucose, U&E, LFTs, calcium, CRP/ESR, coeliac serology with the NG20 gluten caveat ± vit D/B12/folate, pregnancy/HIV per history) rather than a scattergun "test for everything", and explains the rationale

Explores THE LIFE BEHIND IT — mood/anxiety (with a validated tool if indicated), sleep hygiene/pattern, work/relationship/financial stress, alcohol/caffeine, diet, exercise, life events — openly and without judgement
Avoids BOTH errors: neither over-investigates (feeding health anxiety) nor prematurely dismisses as "just stress", holding organic and psychosocial possibilities together as complementary
Offers proportionate management — sleep/lifestyle advice, mood support/treatment if depression/anxiety identified, addressing modifiable factors — alongside the investigation plan

Elicits the hidden agenda (the specific fear or unnamed stressor) with open questions ("what are you most worried it might be?", "what’s life like at the moment?") and validates both the symptom and the fear
Negotiates a proportionate plan with a patient wanting "everything" — explaining why focused testing is better — without leaving her feeling dismissed or fobbed off

Safety-nets and follows up: definite review of results, what red flags warrant sooner contact, a timeframe and plan if first-line tests are normal (review lifestyle/mood, reassess, consider next steps, including ME/CFS if post-exertional malaise persists — NG206: suspect at 6 weeks, diagnose at 3 months), and signposting — balanced thoroughness, neither over-investigation nor premature reassurance

worked.txt: "Four months of being wiped out is genuinely tough, and I want to take it seriously — not just hand you a tonic. Let me understand it properly and then do the right tests, and I also want to understand what life’s like for you at the moment, because both matter."

"Is it more sleepiness, or no energy, or muscles tiring? Worse at any time of day? … And a few specific checks: any weight loss, fevers or night sweats, lumps, breathlessness, or anything new and neurological? … None — that’s reassuring and helps me aim the tests."

"I know it’s tempting to ‘test for everything’, but that actually causes more confusion — false alarms and red herrings. Instead I’ll do a focused set that covers the things that genuinely cause tiredness: blood count and iron, thyroid, blood sugar, kidneys, liver, calcium, inflammation, and coeliac — for that one you need to be eating gluten every day beforehand. I’d like the blood count done in the next couple of days, and I’ll check you over in person when you come in. That’s thorough and sensible."

"Can I ask about the rest of it? How’s your mood — are you still enjoying things? How’s sleep — phone in bed, racing mind? And work and home, any stress or worries? … Tell me more about that." (Listens.)

"What you’re describing sounds like a lot on your plate and some low mood and broken sleep — which can absolutely cause this kind of exhaustion. That’s NOT me saying it’s ‘all in your head’; it’s real, and it’s treatable. The blood tests run alongside that, not instead of it."

"Let’s get the bloods, work on sleep and the stress, and I’d like to see you back to go through results and how you’re doing. If you develop weight loss, fevers, lumps or anything that alarms you in the meantime, come sooner. We’ll get to the bottom of this together."

f.learning: "Tired all the time" (TATT) is common, real and usually multifactorial, and the strong consultation does TWO things at once: a STRUCTURED history with a red-flag screen and a FOCUSED first-line investigation, AND genuine exploration of the life behind the fatigue. Characterise the tiredness (sleepiness vs lack of energy vs muscle fatigue), its duration, pattern and functional impact, and screen red flags (weight loss, fevers/night sweats, lymphadenopathy, breathlessness, focal/neurological symptoms, bleeding, a progressive course) whose presence redirects to urgent investigation. Resist the scattergun "test for everything": a reasonable evidence-based panel is FBC (very urgently, within 48 hours — NICE NG12 (Suspected cancer: recognition and referral, last updated April 2026) advises considering this for persistent fatigue), ferritin, TFTs, HbA1c/glucose, U&E, LFTs, calcium, CRP/ESR and coeliac serology (NG20: only while eating gluten in more than one meal a day for at least 6 weeks), with vitamin D, B12/folate, pregnancy test or HIV added per history — explained, because indiscriminate testing breeds false positives, incidental findings and anxiety. Equally, explore the commonest causes — depression and anxiety, poor sleep, work/relationship/financial stress, alcohol/caffeine, diet and activity, and life events — openly and without judgement, often using "what are you most worried it might be?" and "what’s life like at the moment?" to surface the real driver (a fear, or an unnamed stressor or unrecognised depression). Avoid both errors: over-investigation feeds health anxiety, while prematurely labelling "just stress" risks missing organic disease or invalidating distress — so hold organic and psychosocial possibilities together as complementary, offer proportionate lifestyle/mood support alongside the screen, safety-net for evolving red flags, and arrange a definite review. There is no suspected cancer pathway referral for undifferentiated fatigue without red flags, but NICE NG12 does advise considering a very urgent FBC (within 48 hours) for persistent fatigue, and red-flag safety-netting completes it. If post-exertional malaise persists, NICE NG206: suspect ME/CFS in adults when the key symptoms, including post-exertional malaise, have lasted at least 6 weeks; diagnose only if they persist for 3 months and are not explained by another condition.

knowledge.guideline: NICE NG20 (coeliac disease, 2015) · NICE NG12 Suspected cancer: recognition and referral (2015, last updated 15 April 2026) · NICE NG206 (ME/CFS, 2021) · NICE NG222 (depression in adults, 2022, updated December 2025) · NICE CG113 (generalised anxiety disorder and panic disorder, 2011) · UK CMO low-risk drinking guidelines (2016)
knowledge.summary: Four months of fatigue in a 26-year-old is usually multifactorial, often sleep, mood and stress. Take a structured history, screen red flags, do a focused and explained first-line panel, and explore the life behind it — both, not either.

points.t: Sleepiness, lack of energy and muscle weakness point in different directions. Ask about onset, pattern, sleep quality and functional impact, and about worsening after exertion. NICE NG206: suspect ME/CFS in adults when the key symptoms, including post-exertional malaise, have lasted at least 6 weeks; diagnose only if they persist for 3 months and are not explained by another condition.

Weight loss, fevers or night sweats, lumps, breathlessness, bleeding or bruising, neurological symptoms, or a progressive course redirect the assessment. NICE NG12: consider a very urgent full blood count (within 48 hours) to assess for leukaemia in adults with features including persistent fatigue — so the FBC is done promptly, not left for weeks.

FBC, ferritin, TFTs, HbA1c or glucose, U&E, LFTs, calcium and CRP or ESR, with coeliac serology — NICE NG20 recommends offering it for prolonged fatigue (she must be eating gluten in more than one meal every day for at least 6 weeks before testing). Add a pregnancy test, B12, vitamin D or HIV testing only as the history suggests. Explain the choice: scattergun testing produces false positives and more anxiety.

Depression, anxiety, poor sleep, work stress, late screens, caffeine and alcohol are the commonest contributors. Use a validated tool such as PHQ-9 or GAD-7 where mood or anxiety is suspected. NICE NG222 and CG113: offer treatment matched to severity and preference, including NHS Talking Therapies (self-referral).

Avoid both errors: over-investigating feeds health anxiety; labelling it “just stress” too early risks missing organic disease and leaves the patient feeling dismissed. Present the tests and the psychosocial plan as complementary.

Review results and function in a few weeks. If the first-line tests are normal, reassess the history, sleep and mood rather than widening the panel reflexively; re-examine and re-screen red flags if the picture changes.

dg.d: Open question; took the fatigue seriously before discussing tests.
Work pressure, long hours, screens, sleep, caffeine, alcohol and mood.
Focused panel: FBC, ferritin, TFTs, HbA1c, U&E, LFTs, calcium, CRP, coeliac serology (NICE NG20); pregnancy test offered; PHQ-9/GAD-7.
Anaemia, thyroid, diabetes, coeliac vs sleep disruption, depression, anxiety, stress; ME/CFS features screened (NICE NG206).
Red-flag screen; prompt FBC given persistent fatigue (NICE NG12); no invented cancer referral.
Likely multifactorial fatigue — poor sleep, stress and low mood — pending a focused organic screen.
After open exploration, used closed questions with clear signposting to confirm specific details.
Used information already available in the notes/referral; did not re-ask what was already documented or said.

dg.t: Finishes data gathering in good time
dg.d: History, ICE, psychosocial context and red-flag screen completed by ~6–7 minutes, leaving time for explanation and a shared plan.

cm.d: Explained focused tests; one negotiated sleep change; mood questionnaires; NHS Talking Therapies signposted.
Caffeine, screens and workload addressed; mood treated as real and treatable (NICE NG222, CG113).
Physical and mental-health safety-net; review with results in two to three weeks; teach-back.

cm.t: Uses psychosocial information in the plan
cm.d: Tailored the plan to the patient’s circumstances, beliefs and practical barriers rather than giving a generic plan.

cm.t: Shares risks and safety of options
cm.d: Explained the benefits and risks of the options clearly, as concrete terms or numbers where possible.
Acknowledged autonomy, capacity, confidentiality, safeguarding and any fitness-to-drive/work or duty-of-care implications relevant to this case.
Moved efficiently through the consultation so all key areas were covered within the time without getting stuck.

ro.d: Picked up “something must be really wrong”, “I don’t sleep well” and “a bit flat”, and explored each.
Idea (something serious that tests will find); concern (a serious diagnosis); expectation (every test).
Warm, non-judgmental tone; put the patient at ease and showed respect for their perspective.
Opened broadly and let the patient tell their story before narrowing down.
When a cue was offered, stopped and explored the specific concern rather than reassuring superficially and moving on.
Active listening throughout — reflecting, pausing, not interrupting — interested in the patient as a person.
Told the patient why a question, examination or test was being done — transparent reasoning throughout.
Explained the working diagnosis or analysis in plain language the patient could understand.

ro.t: Shares and uses ICE in the plan
ro.d: Addressed the patient’s specific concern — she fears a serious illness she has read about online; underneath, months of work stress, poor sleep and loneliness since moving that she hasn't connected to the tiredness — directly within the plan, rather than noting it and moving on.
Checked understanding, offered written/follow-up support, asked if anything else was on their mind, agreed next steps.
Clear agenda set early, logical flow from data gathering to management. Did not jump to a plan before gathering enough information.
Explained clinical terms in plain English, or defined them immediately; checked the patient was following.
Noticed and responded to emotional and verbal cues rather than continuing a fixed clinical script.

model.text: Hello Hannah, I’m Dr Lee. Can you see and hear me okay? … Good. Tell me what’s been going on.
model.why: Open question after checking the video link

model.text: I’m just exhausted all the time — it’s been months. I drag myself through work and crash at the weekend. I keep thinking something must be really wrong. Can you just test me for everything — thyroid, iron, anything?

Four months of being wiped out is really tough, and I want to take it seriously. I’d like to understand it properly first, then agree the right tests, and also hear what life is like at the moment, because both matter. Is that okay?
model.why: Validates and sets an agenda that includes both strands

model.text: Okay. As long as we do the tests.
When you say exhausted, is it more sleepiness, no energy, or your muscles giving out?
No energy, mostly. Heavy. And I don’t sleep well.
Tell me about the sleep.
I’m on my laptop until late, then I lie there with my mind racing. I wake up feeling like I haven’t slept.
Does doing something active leave you much worse for a day or more afterwards?
I don’t think so. I just feel flat most of the time.
A few specific checks. Any weight loss without trying, fevers, night sweats, lumps anywhere, breathlessness, unusual bruising or bleeding, or anything like numbness or weakness?
No, none of those.
That’s reassuring and helps me aim the tests. Is there any chance you could be pregnant, and are your periods heavy at all?
model.why: Pregnancy and heavy periods as causes

model.text: I don’t think so. I’m happy to do a test if it helps rule it out.
How much caffeine and alcohol in a typical week?
Lots of coffee to get through the day. Not much alcohol.
How has your mood been — are you still enjoying things?
I suppose I’ve been a bit flat. I haven’t really thought of it like that.
You said you keep thinking something must be really wrong. What are you most worried it might be?
Honestly? Something serious. You read things online and it’s always something awful. I just want someone to find it.
That makes sense — when you feel this bad, it’s natural to fear the worst. And what’s life like at the moment, work and home?
model.why: Validates the fear and opens the psychosocial story

model.text: Work’s been full-on. Deadlines, long hours, always on my phone. I haven’t had a proper break in ages.

Thank you. Here’s how I see it. There’s nothing in what you’ve told me that points to something serious, which is good. I will still do tests, but a focused set, not everything: blood count and iron, thyroid, blood sugar, kidney and liver tests, calcium, an inflammation marker, and a coeliac test. Those cover the physical causes that genuinely cause tiredness at your age.
Why not everything, though? Just to be sure?

Because testing everything gives false alarms — slightly odd results that mean nothing but lead to more tests and more worry. A focused set is more likely to find a real cause if there is one. And if these are normal, that’s genuinely useful information.
Okay, that makes sense.

I also think the late nights on the laptop, broken sleep, heavy workload and feeling flat could be doing a lot of this. That’s not me saying it’s all in your head — it’s real, and it’s treatable. The blood tests run alongside that, not instead of it.
model.why: Holds organic and psychosocial explanations together

model.text: I suppose I’ve been ignoring that side.

Could you fill in two short questionnaires about mood and worry before our next appointment? And for sleep: screens off an hour before bed, a regular wake-up time, and cutting coffee after lunch. Which of those feels most doable?
model.why: Validated tools and one negotiated change

model.text: Screens off earlier, probably. I’ll try.

Good. If the mood side turns out to be bigger than it looks, there’s NHS Talking Therapies, which you can refer yourself to. I’ll book the blood test for this week, and we can add a pregnancy test so it’s ruled out.
model.why: Signposts support and times the tests promptly

model.text: Thank you.

If you notice weight loss, fevers, sweats, lumps, bruising or anything that alarms you before then, contact us sooner. And if you ever feel very low or have thoughts of harming yourself, contact us the same day or call 111.
Okay.
What will you take away from today?
Focused bloods this week, not everything. Screens off earlier and less coffee. Do the questionnaires. Come back to go through it all.
Exactly. Let’s speak again in two to three weeks with the results and see how the sleep is going. We’ll get to the bottom of this together. Anything else?
No — I feel like someone’s actually listening. Thanks.

social.t: Long hours, always-on phones and late laptop use drive poor sleep and exhaustion. Explore what she can change and what her employer could adjust.
Online searching amplifies fear. Acknowledge it, give clear information, and avoid repeated testing as reassurance.

legal.t: She is working. If fatigue later affects work, she can self-certify for the first 7 days; a fit note can then say she “may be fit for work” with adjustments such as altered hours.
Pregnancy and HIV tests need her informed agreement; explain why any test is offered.

professional.t: Explaining why some tests are not done is part of shared decision-making, not rationing (GMC decision making and consent, 2020).
Offer review with the same clinician where possible; continuity reduces repeated testing in undifferentiated symptoms.

community.t: NHS Talking Therapies (self-referral); Every Mind Matters for sleep and stress; Mind for mental-health information.

redFlags: Unintentional weight loss, fevers, night sweats
Lumps, unusual bruising or bleeding, pallor
Breathlessness, neurological symptoms, a progressive course
Low mood with hopelessness or thoughts of self-harm
psychosocial: Work pressure, long hours and screens
Mood and anxiety; fear of a serious diagnosis
ice: Concern: a serious diagnosis being missed

playbook.diagnosis: Four months of fatigue with no red flags, poor sleep, heavy work stress, high caffeine and low mood: most likely multifactorial, with a focused organic screen running alongside. ME/CFS features are screened but not present on this history.
playbook.diagnosisLay: “Your tiredness is real. From what you’ve told me, poor sleep, a very heavy workload and feeling flat are likely doing a lot of it. I’ll also check the physical causes that genuinely cause tiredness, so we cover both sides.”

management.reflectIce: “You’ve been worried something serious is being missed. I’ve asked about all the warning signs, none are there, and the tests I’m doing are the ones that would pick up the physical causes.”
management.psychosocial: Validate the fear; open work and sleep; negotiate one change she owns; offer mood questionnaires and self-referral to NHS Talking Therapies.
sharedPlan: Focused bloods this week: FBC, ferritin, TFTs, HbA1c, U&E, LFTs, calcium, CRP, coeliac serology (NICE NG20)
Sleep: screens off an hour before bed, regular wake time, less caffeine; PHQ-9 and GAD-7
NHS Talking Therapies if mood or anxiety confirmed (NICE NG222, CG113)
safetyNet: Weight loss, fevers, sweats, lumps, bruising — contact sooner
Very low mood or thoughts of self-harm — same day or 111; review with results in two to three weeks

pitfalls.intro: Tiredness stations punish both extremes: the candidate who bleeds everything and the one who says “stress” and stops. The marks are in holding both.

items.fail: Agreeing to “test everything” and requesting a long list of tests without a history.
items.why: “Investigations not appropriate or justified.” Scattergun testing breeds false positives and anxiety.
items.fix: Name a focused panel and explain why it is better than everything.

items.fail: Skipping the red-flag screen because she is young.
items.why: “Did not rule out serious disease.” Weight loss, sweats, lumps and bleeding must be asked about.
items.fix: One sentence covers it: “Any weight loss, fevers, sweats, lumps, bruising or breathlessness?”

items.fail: Telling her it’s probably stress in the first five minutes.
items.why: “Did not explore the patient’s concerns.” She came fearing something serious; she hears dismissal.
items.fix: Ask what she fears most, then explain how the plan answers it.

items.fail: Never asking about life outside the symptom.
items.why: “Did not explore psychosocial factors.” Work, screens and mood are the likely drivers here.
items.fix: “What’s life like at the moment?” — then listen.

items.fail: A lecture on sleep hygiene with ten changes.
items.why: “Did not involve the patient in the plan.”
items.fix: Offer the options and ask which one feels doable.

items.fail: No plan for what happens if the tests are normal.
items.why: Without it, normal results feel like a dead end and drive repeat testing.
items.fix: “If these are normal, that’s useful — we’ll review sleep and mood together and decide next steps.”

timeMap.d: Let her finish. Promise to take it seriously and cover both the tests and life around it.
Type of fatigue, sleep, post-exertional worsening, red flags, pregnancy and periods, caffeine and alcohol, mood.
“What are you most worried it might be?” and “What’s life like at the moment?”
Focused panel with reasons; why not everything. Hold both explanations. One sleep change; mood questionnaires; Talking Therapies.
Physical red flags and low-mood safety-net. Teach-back. Review with results.

wordPics.fail: Orders a huge panel without a history; or tells her it’s probably stress and sends her away without tests; no red-flag screen; mood never explored; no review.
wordPics.pass: Structured history with red-flag screen, focused first-line bloods, some exploration of mood and sleep, basic lifestyle advice and a review.
wordPics.exc: All of the above, plus: draws out her fear and her stressors with open questions; explains why focused testing is better without making her feel dismissed; holds organic and psychosocial causes together; negotiates one owned change; uses validated tools; safety-nets both physical and mental health.

SCA_KNOWLEDGE.guideline: NICE NG20 (coeliac disease, 2015) · NICE NG12 Suspected cancer: recognition and referral (2015, last updated 15 April 2026) · NICE NG206 (ME/CFS, 2021) · NICE NG222 (depression in adults, 2022, updated December 2025) · NICE CG113 (generalised anxiety disorder and panic disorder, 2011) · UK CMO low-risk drinking guidelines (2016)
SCA_KNOWLEDGE.summary: Four months of fatigue in a 26-year-old is usually multifactorial, often sleep, mood and stress. Take a structured history, screen red flags, do a focused and explained first-line panel, and explore the life behind it — both, not either.

points.t: Sleepiness, lack of energy and muscle weakness point in different directions. Ask about onset, pattern, sleep quality and functional impact, and about worsening after exertion. NICE NG206: suspect ME/CFS in adults when the key symptoms, including post-exertional malaise, have lasted at least 6 weeks; diagnose only if they persist for 3 months and are not explained by another condition.

Weight loss, fevers or night sweats, lumps, breathlessness, bleeding or bruising, neurological symptoms, or a progressive course redirect the assessment. NICE NG12: consider a very urgent full blood count (within 48 hours) to assess for leukaemia in adults with features including persistent fatigue — so the FBC is done promptly, not left for weeks.

FBC, ferritin, TFTs, HbA1c or glucose, U&E, LFTs, calcium and CRP or ESR, with coeliac serology — NICE NG20 recommends offering it for prolonged fatigue (she must be eating gluten in more than one meal every day for at least 6 weeks before testing). Add a pregnancy test, B12, vitamin D or HIV testing only as the history suggests. Explain the choice: scattergun testing produces false positives and more anxiety.

Depression, anxiety, poor sleep, work stress, late screens, caffeine and alcohol are the commonest contributors. Use a validated tool such as PHQ-9 or GAD-7 where mood or anxiety is suspected. NICE NG222 and CG113: offer treatment matched to severity and preference, including NHS Talking Therapies (self-referral).

Avoid both errors: over-investigating feeds health anxiety; labelling it “just stress” too early risks missing organic disease and leaves the patient feeling dismissed. Present the tests and the psychosocial plan as complementary.

Review results and function in a few weeks. If the first-line tests are normal, reassess the history, sleep and mood rather than widening the panel reflexively; re-examine and re-screen red flags if the picture changes.

SCA_SC_TASKS.d: Open question; took the fatigue seriously before discussing tests.
Work pressure, long hours, screens, sleep, caffeine, alcohol and mood.
Picked up “something must be really wrong”, “I don’t sleep well” and “a bit flat”, and explored each.
Idea (something serious that tests will find); concern (a serious diagnosis); expectation (every test).
Focused panel: FBC, ferritin, TFTs, HbA1c, U&E, LFTs, calcium, CRP, coeliac serology (NICE NG20); pregnancy test offered; PHQ-9/GAD-7.
Anaemia, thyroid, diabetes, coeliac vs sleep disruption, depression, anxiety, stress; ME/CFS features screened (NICE NG206).
Red-flag screen; prompt FBC given persistent fatigue (NICE NG12); no invented cancer referral.
Likely multifactorial fatigue — poor sleep, stress and low mood — pending a focused organic screen.
Explained focused tests; one negotiated sleep change; mood questionnaires; NHS Talking Therapies signposted.
Caffeine, screens and workload addressed; mood treated as real and treatable (NICE NG222, CG113).
Physical and mental-health safety-net; review with results in two to three weeks; teach-back.

social.t: Long hours, always-on phones and late laptop use drive poor sleep and exhaustion. Explore what she can change and what her employer could adjust.
Online searching amplifies fear. Acknowledge it, give clear information, and avoid repeated testing as reassurance.

legal.t: She is working. If fatigue later affects work, she can self-certify for the first 7 days; a fit note can then say she “may be fit for work” with adjustments such as altered hours.
Pregnancy and HIV tests need her informed agreement; explain why any test is offered.

professional.t: Explaining why some tests are not done is part of shared decision-making, not rationing (GMC decision making and consent, 2020).
Offer review with the same clinician where possible; continuity reduces repeated testing in undifferentiated symptoms.

community.t: NHS Talking Therapies (self-referral); Every Mind Matters for sleep and stress; Mind for mental-health information.

redFlags: Unintentional weight loss, fevers, night sweats
Lumps, unusual bruising or bleeding, pallor
Breathlessness, neurological symptoms, a progressive course
Low mood with hopelessness or thoughts of self-harm
psychosocial: Work pressure, long hours and screens
Mood and anxiety; fear of a serious diagnosis
ice: Concern: a serious diagnosis being missed

SCA_PLAYBOOK.diagnosis: Four months of fatigue with no red flags, poor sleep, heavy work stress, high caffeine and low mood: most likely multifactorial, with a focused organic screen running alongside. ME/CFS features are screened but not present on this history.
SCA_PLAYBOOK.diagnosisLay: “Your tiredness is real. From what you’ve told me, poor sleep, a very heavy workload and feeling flat are likely doing a lot of it. I’ll also check the physical causes that genuinely cause tiredness, so we cover both sides.”

management.reflectIce: “You’ve been worried something serious is being missed. I’ve asked about all the warning signs, none are there, and the tests I’m doing are the ones that would pick up the physical causes.”
management.psychosocial: Validate the fear; open work and sleep; negotiate one change she owns; offer mood questionnaires and self-referral to NHS Talking Therapies.
sharedPlan: Focused bloods this week: FBC, ferritin, TFTs, HbA1c, U&E, LFTs, calcium, CRP, coeliac serology (NICE NG20)
Sleep: screens off an hour before bed, regular wake time, less caffeine; PHQ-9 and GAD-7
NHS Talking Therapies if mood or anxiety confirmed (NICE NG222, CG113)
safetyNet: Weight loss, fevers, sweats, lumps, bruising — contact sooner
Very low mood or thoughts of self-harm — same day or 111; review with results in two to three weeks

SCA_PITFALLS.intro: Tiredness stations punish both extremes: the candidate who bleeds everything and the one who says “stress” and stops. The marks are in holding both.

items.fail: Agreeing to “test everything” and requesting a long list of tests without a history.
items.why: “Investigations not appropriate or justified.” Scattergun testing breeds false positives and anxiety.
items.fix: Name a focused panel and explain why it is better than everything.

items.fail: Skipping the red-flag screen because she is young.
items.why: “Did not rule out serious disease.” Weight loss, sweats, lumps and bleeding must be asked about.
items.fix: One sentence covers it: “Any weight loss, fevers, sweats, lumps, bruising or breathlessness?”

items.fail: Telling her it’s probably stress in the first five minutes.
items.why: “Did not explore the patient’s concerns.” She came fearing something serious; she hears dismissal.
items.fix: Ask what she fears most, then explain how the plan answers it.

items.fail: Never asking about life outside the symptom.
items.why: “Did not explore psychosocial factors.” Work, screens and mood are the likely drivers here.
items.fix: “What’s life like at the moment?” — then listen.

items.fail: A lecture on sleep hygiene with ten changes.
items.why: “Did not involve the patient in the plan.”
items.fix: Offer the options and ask which one feels doable.

items.fail: No plan for what happens if the tests are normal.
items.why: Without it, normal results feel like a dead end and drive repeat testing.
items.fix: “If these are normal, that’s useful — we’ll review sleep and mood together and decide next steps.”
